meta.title: Who really said "All compounded things are subject to decay. Strive with diligence"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The Buddha's last words really are in the Pali Canon (Digha Nikaya 16) — but this exact English wording matches no published translation. What the sutta says.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'All compounded things are subject to decay. Strive with diligence'?
meta.ogDescription: The sentence is canonical — Digha Nikaya 16 records it as the Buddha's final words. The popular English wording, though, belongs to no identified translator.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 6th or 5th century BCE · Founder of Buddhism
answer.sourceLine: The sentence really is in the Pali Canon: the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 16) records “vayadhammā saṅkhārā appamādena sampādethā” as the Buddha’s final words at Kusinara. But this particular English wording matches no published translation we could identify — the standard renderings read “subject to vanish … strive with earnestness,” “subject to ending & decay … reach consummation through heedfulness,” or “work out your salvation with diligence.”

source.heading: The last words at Kusinara

docMeta.dd: The Buddha’s final words, chapter 6 — numbered 6:8 in the Buddhist Publication Society edition, §10 in Rhys Davids, 6.7 at SuttaCentral
“Handa dāni, bhikkhave, āmantayāmi vo: vayadhammā saṅkhārā appamādena sampādethā”
None identified for the popular wording. Published renderings differ — see the trail below.

source.excerpt: Then the Blessed One addressed the brethren, and said, ‘Behold now, brethren, I exhort you, saying, “Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!”’ This was the last word of the Tathagata!
trail: The Pali behind every English version is vayadhammā saṅkhārā appamādena sampādetha, transcribed in note 58 to Access to Insight’s DN 16 ↗, where part 6 §8 adds: “This was the last word of the Tathagata.”

The published Buddhist Publication Society translation by Sister Vajira and Francis Story reads “All compounded things are subject to vanish. Strive with earnestness!” — vanish and earnestness, not decay and diligence (Access to Insight ↗, from the 1998 revised edition).

Thanissaro Bhikkhu’s translation ↗ gives “All fabrications are subject to ending & decay. Reach consummation through heedfulness,” and Bhikkhu Sujato’s ↗ compresses it to “Conditions fall apart. Persist with diligence.”

Wikiquote ↗ lists the popular wording under “Miscellaneous” and cites it to DN 16 6:8, but supplies no translator for it. Quote Investigator ↗ returns nothing for the phrase — it has never investigated this line.
source.excerptNote: From T. W. Rhys Davids’ public-domain translation in Buddhist Suttas, Sacred Books of the East vol. XI (Clarendon Press, 1900). This is the same Pali sentence the popular quote renders — but note that neither “compounded things” nor “strive” appears here.

source.rightsNote: We cannot assign a rights status to the wording shown, because we could not identify the translator who produced it — and rights in a translated text belong to the translation, not the ancient original. Two flanking cases are clear: T. W. Rhys Davids’ rendering in Sacred Books of the East vol. XI (Clarendon Press, 1900) is public domain, while the Sister Vajira and Francis Story translation is © 1998 Buddhist Publication Society and remains in copyright. Treat the popular sentence as of unknown provenance rather than assuming it is free to reuse.

author.name: Gautama Buddha
author.heading: The man who actually said something like this
author.metaLine: 6th or 5th century BCE · Wandering ascetic and teacher in the Indo-Gangetic Plain; founder of Buddhism
author.bio: Siddhartha Gautama — the Buddha — was a wandering ascetic and religious teacher who lived in the eastern Indo-Gangetic Plain during the 6th or 5th century BCE and founded Buddhism. Tradition holds that he renounced a princely household, attained awakening at Bodh Gaya, and spent the rest of his life teaching and building a monastic order. He is said to have died at Kushinagar, and the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta is the canonical account of those final months — the longest discourse in the Pali Canon and the source of every version of this quote.

cite.sourceCitation: Documented in the Pali Canon: Dīgha Nikāya 16, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, ch. 6. Public-domain rendering: T. W. Rhys Davids, trans., “The Book of the Great Decease,” in Buddhist Suttas, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 11 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1900), ch. 6, §10 — “Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!” Modern rendering: Last Days of the Buddha: The Maha-parinibbana Sutta, rev. ed., trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story (Kandy: Buddhist Publication Society, 1998), 6:8. The popular wording “All compounded things are subject to decay. Strive with diligence” matches neither, and no identified translator claims it.

copyAttribution: All compounded things are subject to decay. Strive with diligence. — attributed to Gautama Buddha. A popular English rendering of his last words in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16), where the Pali reads 'vayadhamma sankhara appamadena sampadetha'. No published translation uses this exact wording. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Right speaker, borrowed wording
misattribution.intro: This is the rare Buddha quote that survives scrutiny: the sentence genuinely is in the Pali Canon, in the discourse that narrates his death. What does not survive scrutiny is the English. The version that circulates is a blend of phrases from at least three different translations, and no translator has ever published it in this form.

items.who: “All compounded things are subject to decay. Strive with diligence”
items.why: No published translation located uses this sentence. “All compounded things” comes from the Buddhist Publication Society edition, which continues “are subject to vanish. Strive with earnestness!” — see Access to Insight, DN 16 part 6 §8 ↗. “Subject to decay” echoes Thanissaro Bhikkhu ↗, whose version ends “Reach consummation through heedfulness.”

Wikiquote ↗ heads the entry with this exact wording and cites it to “DN 16; Mahaparinibbana Sutta 6:8” without naming a translator — then lists the genuine published renderings underneath as “variant translations,” inverting which one is actually documented.

The best-known English version, from T. W. Rhys Davids' translation in Sacred Books of the East, vol. XI ↗: “Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!” It is a real, citable translation — but “salvation” has no counterpart in the Pali, which reads only appamādena sampādetha.

Wikiquote also records a very different Victorian paraphrase — “the parts and powers of man must be dissolved; work out your own salvation with diligence” — as quoted in Present Day Tracts on the Non-Christian Religions of the World (1887), p. 24, per Wikiquote ↗. We have not independently examined Muir's book.

misattribution.truthLine: The Buddha really did say this, as the Pali Canon records it: vayadhammā saṅkhārā appamādena sampādethā, DN 16, ch. 6 — “This was the last word of the Tathagata,” per Access to Insight ↗. The English sentence people share, however, belongs to no translator on record.

context.heading: One word, forty-five years
lead: The scene is Kusinara, in a grove of sal trees. The Buddha has just asked the assembled monks three times whether anyone has a lingering doubt about the teaching, the path or the practice. Three times, nobody speaks. He then delivers a single sentence — two clauses, eleven Pali syllables — and says nothing further. The sutta marks the moment flatly: these were the Realized One’s last words.

Everything hangs on appamāda, the word at the centre of the second clause. English translators have reached for “earnestness,” “heedfulness,” “diligence” and “vigilance,” and none of them is quite it. The classical commentary quoted in the notes to Access to Insight’s edition ↗ reads the line as the Buddha compressing forty-five years of teaching into that one word. Which is exactly why the English keeps drifting: there is no single English word carrying the load, so every generation of translators picks a different one — and the version that went viral picked two that no translator actually published together.
context.detailsSummary: Why the same Pali line reads four different ways in English
detailsBody: The Pali is vayadhammā saṅkhārā appamādena sampādethā. Saṅkhārā has no clean English equivalent — Rhys Davids used “component things,” the Buddhist Publication Society edition “compounded things,” Thanissaro Bhikkhu “fabrications,” Bhikkhu Sujato simply “conditions.” Vaya covers decay, vanishing and falling apart at once.

The same formula appears earlier in the sutta too, at DN 16:3.51, spoken at Vesali three months before his death — so the line is not unique to the deathbed scene, which is one reason section numbers cited for it vary between editions.

Rhys Davids’ Victorian “Work out your salvation with diligence” imports a word — salvation — with no counterpart in the Pali, which says only sampādetha, “accomplish” or “bring to completion.” It remains the most-quoted English version anyway, because it was the first widely available one.
context.pull: Three times he asked if anyone had a question. Three times, silence. Then one sentence.
